# The blanket conjecture is FALSE (boundary of the instability theorem)

The research mission's headline claim is

> "For any Cayley digraph `G` of an abelian group of even order, the pair
> `(G, K₂)` is unstable."

This file **refutes** that blanket claim with an explicit, machine-checked
counterexample, and thereby pins down the exact boundary of the positive
results in `Instability.lean`.

## Main result

* `cay_Z4_01_stable` — every automorphism of the double cover of
  `Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is of the expected form; equivalently `Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is
  **stable**.
* `blanket_conjecture_false` — consequently there *is* an even-order abelian
  Cayley digraph that is not unstable, so the blanket conjecture fails.

`Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is connected (the generator `1` already connects all of `ℤ₄`)
and non-bipartite (the loop `0 ∈ S` gives odd closed walks), so the
counterexample is not a degenerate "disconnected/bipartite" artefact.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Experiment (Stage 2): exhaustive computation over all `S ⊆ ℤ₄` (see
`ComputationalEvidence.md`) found `|Aut(BX)| = 2·|Aut(X)|` exactly for
`S ∈ {{0,1},{0,3},{1,2},{2,3},{1,2,3}}`.  The smallest is `S = {0,1}`.

Analysis (Stage 3): classification of even-order circulants.
  * `χ(S)` constant (`S` in the even subgroup, or `S` entirely odd) ⇒ unstable
    — this is the *true* core, proved constructively in `Instability.lean`.
  * `χ(S)` mixed ⇒ instability is genuinely *not* automatic; `{0,1}` is stable
    while `{0,1,2}` is unstable.  So the blanket claim is FALSE, and parity of
    the connection set alone does not decide stability.

Critique (Stage 4): the witness here uses `native_decide` (a finite search over
the 40320 permutations of the 8-vertex double cover).  It is deliberately a
*secondary* result; the main theorems of this development are the constructive,
search-free instability theorems in `Instability.lean`.  The finite check is
the most honest certificate of a *negative* (universally quantified over all
automorphisms) statement.
-/
import Mathlib
import Applications.CayleyDoubleCover.Core

namespace CayleyDoubleCover.Boundary

open CayleyDoubleCover

/-- The connection set `{0, 1}` of the circulant on `ℤ₄`. -/
def S01 : Finset (ZMod 4) := {0, 1}

instance : DecidablePred (IsDCAut S01) := fun e => by unfold IsDCAut; infer_instance
instance : DecidablePred (IsExpected (A := ZMod 4)) := fun e => by
  unfold IsExpected; infer_instance

/-- **Stability of `Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})`.**
Every automorphism of its canonical double cover has the expected form
`(a,i) ↦ (σ a, i ⊕ ε)`.  Verified by exhaustive search over the symmetric group
on the 8 vertices of the double cover. -/
theorem cay_Z4_01_stable :
    ∀ e : Equiv.Perm (ZMod 4 × Bool), IsDCAut S01 e → IsExpected e := by
  native_decide

/-- `Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is **not** unstable. -/
theorem not_unstable_S01 : ¬ Unstable S01 := by
  rintro ⟨e, hAut, hExp⟩
  exact hExp (cay_Z4_01_stable e hAut)

/-- **The blanket conjecture is false.**
There is an even-order abelian Cayley digraph whose pair with `K₂` is *stable*:
`ℤ₄` has even order, `2 ∣ 4`, yet `Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is not unstable. -/
theorem blanket_conjecture_false :
    ∃ (n : ℕ), (2 ∣ n) ∧ ∃ (S : Finset (ZMod n)), ¬ Unstable S :=
  ⟨4, by norm_num, S01, not_unstable_S01⟩

end CayleyDoubleCover.Boundary

# Stability of Cayley Digraphs and their Canonical Double Cover (Core definitions)

This file sets up a self-contained, *computable* framework for studying the
**stability** of a Cayley digraph `Cay(A, S)` of a (finite) abelian group `A`
under the canonical double cover operation `· × K₂`.

## The objects

* Vertices of `Cay(A, S)` are the elements of `A`; there is an arc `a → b`
  iff `b - a ∈ S`.
* The **canonical double cover** (a.k.a. tensor product with `K₂`,
  the "bipartite double") has vertex set `A × Bool`, with an arc
  `p → q` iff `p.2 ≠ q.2` (we cross the two layers) and `q.1 - p.1 ∈ S`.
  This is `DCadj`.
* An **automorphism** of the double cover is a permutation of `A × Bool`
  preserving `DCadj` (`IsDCAut`).
* Every double cover automatically carries the "expected" automorphisms
  `(a, i) ↦ (σ a, i ⊕ ε)` coming from `Aut(Cay(A,S)) × ℤ₂` (`IsExpected`).
* `Cay(A, S)` is **unstable** when there is an automorphism of its double
  cover that is *not* of the expected form (`Unstable`).  This is exactly the
  statement `Aut(Cay(A,S) × K₂) ≠ Aut(Cay(A,S)) × ℤ₂`.

All predicates are kept `Decidable` (no `Classical`) so that concrete instances
can be settled by `decide` / `native_decide` in `Boundary.lean`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Stage 1): "(G, K₂) is unstable for every Cayley digraph G of an
abelian group of even order."  To even *state* this we need a faithful, finite,
decidable model of the double cover and of the splitting `Aut(X) × ℤ₂`.

Experiment (Stage 2): we modelled the double cover on `A × Bool` with the
single uniform arc rule `p.2 ≠ q.2 ∧ q.1 - p.1 ∈ S` (valid for *digraphs*,
not just graphs — we do **not** assume `S = -S`).  A short brute force over
`ℤ₄, ℤ₆` (see `ComputationalEvidence.md`) confirmed the model reproduces the
known automorphism counts, e.g. `|Aut(Cay(ℤ₄,{1}) × K₂)| = 32`.

Analysis (Stage 3): the *expected* subgroup is precisely the image of the
homomorphism `Aut(X) × ℤ₂ → Aut(X × K₂)`, whose elements have the rigid shape
`(a,i) ↦ (σ a, i ⊕ ε)`; instability ⇔ this map is not surjective.
-/
import Mathlib

namespace CayleyDoubleCover

variable {A : Type*} [AddCommGroup A]

/-- Adjacency of the canonical double cover of `Cay(A, S)`:
there is an arc `p → q` iff the two `Bool`-layers differ and `q.1 - p.1 ∈ S`. -/
def DCadj (S : Finset A) (p q : A × Bool) : Prop :=
  p.2 ≠ q.2 ∧ (q.1 - p.1 ∈ S)

instance (S : Finset A) [DecidableEq A] : DecidableRel (DCadj S) := fun p q => by
  unfold DCadj; infer_instance

/-- A double-cover automorphism: a permutation of `A × Bool` preserving `DCadj`. -/
def IsDCAut (S : Finset A) (e : Equiv.Perm (A × Bool)) : Prop :=
  ∀ p q, DCadj S (e p) (e q) ↔ DCadj S p q

/-- The "expected" automorphisms coming from `Aut(Cay(A,S)) × ℤ₂`:
those of the form `(a, i) ↦ (σ a, i ⊕ ε)` for a fixed permutation `σ` of `A`
and a fixed `ε : Bool` (the deck transformation flag). -/
def IsExpected (e : Equiv.Perm (A × Bool)) : Prop :=
  ∃ (σ : Equiv.Perm A) (ε : Bool), ∀ p : A × Bool, e p = (σ p.1, xor p.2 ε)

/-- `Cay(A, S)` is **unstable** iff its canonical double cover has an
automorphism that is not of the expected form. -/
def Unstable (S : Finset A) : Prop :=
  ∃ e, IsDCAut S e ∧ ¬ IsExpected e

/-- The candidate "unexpected" automorphism attached to a parity character
`χ : A → Bool`: it fixes the first coordinate and flips the layer of `(a,i)`
exactly when `χ a = true`.  It is always an involution, hence a permutation. -/
def chiSwap (χ : A → Bool) : Equiv.Perm (A × Bool) where
  toFun p := (p.1, xor p.2 (χ p.1))
  invFun p := (p.1, xor p.2 (χ p.1))
  left_inv p := by simp
  right_inv p := by simp

omit [AddCommGroup A] in
@[simp] lemma chiSwap_apply (χ : A → Bool) (p : A × Bool) :
    chiSwap χ p = (p.1, xor p.2 (χ p.1)) := rfl

end CayleyDoubleCover

# Instability of Cayley digraphs via a parity character (Main results)

This is the positive half of the study.  We isolate a *sharp, constructive*
sufficient condition for the canonical double cover of a Cayley digraph
`Cay(A, S)` to be unstable, and we specialise it to the even-order (cyclic)
case, which is the setting of the research mission.

## Main results

* `cayley_dc_unstable` — **abstract criterion.**  If `A` carries a parity
  character `χ : A → Bool` (an additive map onto `Bool` with `xor`) whose
  kernel contains the connection set `S`, then `Cay(A, S)` is unstable.  The
  explicit unexpected automorphism is `chiSwap χ : (a,i) ↦ (a, i ⊕ χ a)`.
* `cayley_dc_unstable_of_hom` — the same, phrased with a surjective additive
  homomorphism `f : A →+ ZMod 2`.
* `circulant_dc_unstable` — **even cyclic groups.**  For `2 ∣ n` and any
  connection set `S` lying in the even subgroup `ker(ℤ_n → ℤ₂)`, the circulant
  `Cay(ℤ_n, S)` is unstable.
* `circulant_dc_unstable_oddCap` — the **cross-domain bridge**: the same
  conclusion with "even order" packaged through the *Algebra*-domain parity
  predicate `oddCap` of `Algebra/ConformabilityOddOrder.lean`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Stage 1): the blanket claim "every even-order abelian Cayley
digraph is unstable".  Stage-2 brute force (`ComputationalEvidence.md`) shows
this is **false** (see `Boundary.lean`), but reveals a clean *true* core:
whenever the connection set `S` lies inside a parity-character kernel, the map
`(a,i) ↦ (a, i ⊕ χ a)` is an unexpected automorphism.

Experiment (Stage 2): we verified computationally (over ℤ₄, ℤ₆, ℤ₈) that
`chiSwap χ` is a genuine double-cover automorphism **iff** `χ(S) = {false}`,
i.e. `S ⊆ ker χ`, and that it is never of the expected form because `χ` is
surjective (so the layer-flip depends genuinely on the vertex).

Analysis (Stage 3): the proof needs exactly three algebraic facts about `χ`:
additivity (`hadd`), `χ 0 = false`, and surjectivity.  Additivity transports
"`q.1 - p.1 ∈ S`" (hence `χ(q.1 - p.1) = false`) into "`χ q.1 = χ p.1`", which
is what makes the layer-flip respect adjacency.  Surjectivity is what forbids
`chiSwap χ` from collapsing to a global deck flip `(a,i) ↦ (σ a, i ⊕ ε)`.

Critique (Stage 4): the hypothesis `S ⊆ ker χ` makes `Cay(A,S)` disconnected
(it lives in the index-2 subgroup); this is the *honest* boundary of the
construction.  The complementary "bipartite" case `χ(S) = {true}` and the
genuinely connected stable examples are charted in `Boundary.lean`.

Bridge (Stage 5): `circulant_dc_unstable_oddCap` imports `oddCap` from the
**Algebra** domain (`Algebra/ConformabilityOddOrder.lean`) and combines it with
the **Applications/Combinatorics** double-cover construction here: the single
inequality `oddCap n < n` is exactly the even-order hypothesis `2 ∣ n ∧ 0 < n`
that powers the parity character, linking parity arithmetic to digraph
symmetry.
-/
import Mathlib
import Applications.CayleyDoubleCover.Core
import Algebra.ConformabilityOddOrder

namespace CayleyDoubleCover

variable {A : Type*} [AddCommGroup A]

/-- **Abstract instability criterion.**
If `χ : A → Bool` is additive (with respect to `xor`), sends `0` to `false`,
is surjective onto `Bool`, and its kernel contains every element of `S`, then
`Cay(A, S)` is unstable: `chiSwap χ` is an unexpected automorphism of the
canonical double cover. -/
theorem cayley_dc_unstable
    (S : Finset A) (χ : A → Bool)
    (hadd : ∀ a b, χ (a + b) = xor (χ a) (χ b))
    (hzero : χ 0 = false)
    (hsurj : ∃ a, χ a = true)
    (hker : ∀ s ∈ S, χ s = false) :
    Unstable S := by
  refine ⟨chiSwap χ, ?_, ?_⟩
  · -- `chiSwap χ` preserves adjacency.
    intro p q
    simp only [DCadj, chiSwap_apply]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩
      refine ⟨?_, h2⟩
      have hχ : χ q.1 = χ p.1 := by
        have hs := hker _ h2
        have key : χ (p.1 + (q.1 - p.1)) = xor (χ p.1) (χ (q.1 - p.1)) := hadd _ _
        rw [add_sub_cancel, hs] at key; simp [key]
      rw [hχ] at h1; revert h1; cases p.2 <;> cases q.2 <;> simp
    · rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩
      refine ⟨?_, h2⟩
      have hχ : χ q.1 = χ p.1 := by
        have hs := hker _ h2
        have key : χ (p.1 + (q.1 - p.1)) = xor (χ p.1) (χ (q.1 - p.1)) := hadd _ _
        rw [add_sub_cancel, hs] at key; simp [key]
      rw [hχ]; revert h1; cases p.2 <;> cases q.2 <;> simp
  · -- `chiSwap χ` is not of expected form.
    rintro ⟨σ, ε, h⟩
    obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := hsurj
    have h0 := h (0, false)
    have ha2 := h (a, false)
    simp [hzero, ha] at h0 ha2
    rcases h0 with ⟨_, hε0⟩
    rcases ha2 with ⟨_, hε1⟩
    rw [hε0] at hε1; exact absurd hε1 (by decide)

/-- The parity character attached to an additive homomorphism `f : A →+ ZMod 2`. -/
def parityChar (f : A →+ ZMod 2) (a : A) : Bool := decide (f a = 1)

private lemma zmod2_add_xor :
    ∀ x y : ZMod 2, decide (x + y = 1) = xor (decide (x = 1)) (decide (y = 1)) := by
  decide

lemma parityChar_add (f : A →+ ZMod 2) (a b : A) :
    parityChar f (a + b) = xor (parityChar f a) (parityChar f b) := by
  unfold parityChar; rw [map_add]; exact zmod2_add_xor _ _

lemma parityChar_zero (f : A →+ ZMod 2) : parityChar f 0 = false := by
  unfold parityChar; rw [map_zero]; decide

lemma parityChar_surj (f : A →+ ZMod 2) (hf : Function.Surjective f) :
    ∃ a, parityChar f a = true := by
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := hf 1
  exact ⟨a, by unfold parityChar; rw [ha]; decide⟩

/-- **Instability from a surjective additive character.**
If there is a surjective `f : A →+ ZMod 2` whose kernel contains `S`, then
`Cay(A, S)` is unstable. -/
theorem cayley_dc_unstable_of_hom
    (S : Finset A) (f : A →+ ZMod 2) (hf : Function.Surjective f)
    (hker : ∀ s ∈ S, f s = 0) :
    Unstable S := by
  refine cayley_dc_unstable S (parityChar f) (parityChar_add f) (parityChar_zero f)
    (parityChar_surj f hf) ?_
  intro s hs
  unfold parityChar; rw [hker s hs]; decide

/-- **Even cyclic groups (circulants).**
If `2 ∣ n` and every element of `S` lies in the even subgroup
`ker(ℤ_n → ℤ₂)`, then the circulant `Cay(ℤ_n, S)` is unstable. -/
theorem circulant_dc_unstable
    (n : ℕ) (h2 : (2 : ℕ) ∣ n) (S : Finset (ZMod n))
    (hker : ∀ s ∈ S, (ZMod.castHom h2 (ZMod 2)) s = 0) :
    Unstable S := by
  refine cayley_dc_unstable_of_hom S (ZMod.castHom h2 (ZMod 2)).toAddMonoidHom ?_ hker
  exact ZMod.castHom_surjective h2

/-- `oddCap n < n` is exactly the statement that `n` is a positive even number,
the even-order hypothesis we need.  (Algebra-domain bridge lemma.) -/
lemma two_dvd_of_oddCap_lt
    (n : ℕ) (hn : Catalog.Algebra.Conformability.oddCap n < n) : (2 : ℕ) ∣ n := by
  unfold Catalog.Algebra.Conformability.oddCap at hn
  split at hn
  · omega
  · rename_i h; rw [Nat.not_odd_iff_even] at h; exact h.two_dvd

/-- **Cross-domain bridge (Algebra ⊕ Applications/Combinatorics).**
The even-order hypothesis is packaged through the `Algebra`-domain parity
predicate `oddCap` of `Algebra/ConformabilityOddOrder.lean`: a positive integer
`n` is even precisely when `oddCap n < n`.  Here `oddCap` is genuinely
load-bearing — it is the *only* source of the divisibility `2 ∣ n` that builds
the parity character.  The connection set is required to consist of *even*
elements (`s = 2 • t`), i.e. to lie in the index-2 even subgroup; under that
hypothesis every such circulant is unstable. -/
theorem circulant_dc_unstable_oddCap
    (n : ℕ) (hn : Catalog.Algebra.Conformability.oddCap n < n)
    (S : Finset (ZMod n))
    (hker : ∀ s ∈ S, ∃ t : ZMod n, (2 : ZMod n) * t = s) :
    Unstable S := by
  have h2 : (2 : ℕ) ∣ n := two_dvd_of_oddCap_lt n hn
  refine circulant_dc_unstable n h2 S ?_
  intro s hs
  obtain ⟨t, ht⟩ := hker s hs
  rw [← ht, map_mul]
  have : (ZMod.castHom h2 (ZMod 2)) 2 = 0 := by
    rw [map_ofNat]; decide
  rw [this, zero_mul]

end CayleyDoubleCover

# Computational Evidence: Stability of Cayley Digraphs and the `× K₂` Double Cover

All computations below were run by brute force (exhaustive permutation search)
over small abelian groups, *before* the Lean formalization, to decide whether
the mission's blanket claim is true and to locate the true core.

## Model

For `Cay(ℤₙ, S)` we build:
* the digraph `X` on `ℤₙ` with arc `a → b ⟺ (b − a) mod n ∈ S`;
* the canonical double cover `BX = X × K₂` on `ℤₙ × {0,1}` with arc
  `(a,i) → (b,j) ⟺ i ≠ j ∧ (b − a) mod n ∈ S`.

A digraph is **stable** iff `|Aut(BX)| = 2·|Aut(X)|` (the expected subgroup
`Aut(X) × ℤ₂` always embeds, so equality ⟺ no unexpected automorphism).

## 1. Exhaustive scan over `ℤ₂` and `ℤ₄`

Every `S ⊆ ℤ₄`, with `|Aut(X)|`, `|Aut(BX)|`, and verdict:

| S          | \|Aut X\| | \|Aut BX\| | verdict   | χ(S) parity |
|------------|----------:|-----------:|-----------|-------------|
| {}         | 24        | 40320      | unstable  | (empty)     |
| {0}        | 24        | 384        | unstable  | {0}         |
| {1}        | 4         | 32         | unstable  | {1}         |
| {2}        | 8         | 384        | unstable  | {0}         |
| {3}        | 4         | 32         | unstable  | {1}         |
| {0,1}      | 4         | 8          | **STABLE**| {0,1} mixed |
| {0,2}      | 8         | 128        | unstable  | {0}         |
| {0,3}      | 4         | 8          | **STABLE**| {0,1} mixed |
| {1,2}      | 4         | 8          | **STABLE**| {0,1} mixed |
| {1,3}      | 8         | 128        | unstable  | {1}         |
| {2,3}      | 4         | 8          | **STABLE**| {0,1} mixed |
| {0,1,2}    | 4         | 16         | unstable  | {0,1} mixed |
| {0,1,3}    | 8         | 48         | unstable  | {0,1} mixed |
| {0,2,3}    | 4         | 16         | unstable  | {0,1} mixed |
| {1,2,3}    | 24        | 48         | **STABLE**| {0,1} mixed |
| {0,1,2,3}  | 24        | 1152       | unstable  | {0,1} mixed |

(All `S ⊆ ℤ₂` are unstable, but only via disconnected/bipartite double covers.)

### Key reads

* **Counterexample to the blanket claim.** `Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is stable
  (`|Aut BX| = 8 = 2·4`). It is connected (`1` generates `ℤ₄`) and
  non-bipartite (loop `0 ∈ S`). ⇒ "even order ⇒ unstable" is **false**.
  This is the smallest counterexample; formalized in `Boundary.lean`.

* **True sufficient core.** Whenever the parity `χ(S) = {x mod 2 : x ∈ S}` is
  *constant* (all even, or all odd), the digraph is unstable in every row above.
  The "all even" case (`S` in the even subgroup) is proved in full generality
  in `Instability.lean` via the explicit automorphism `(a,i) ↦ (a, i ⊕ χ a)`.

* **Parity does not decide stability.** When `χ(S)` is *mixed*, both verdicts
  occur (`{0,1}` stable, `{0,1,2}` unstable). So stability is strictly subtler
  than connection-set parity.

## 2. Direct verification of the formal construction

For the construction `f(a,i) = (a, i ⊕ (a mod 2))` used in `Instability.lean`,
we checked over `ℤ₄, ℤ₆, ℤ₈` that `f` is a genuine double-cover automorphism and
is never of the expected form, **exactly** when `S` lies in the even subgroup:

```
n=4 S=[0,2]   chi(S)={0}  f_is_aut=True   f_expected=False  => unstable witness
n=4 S=[1,3]   chi(S)={1}  f_is_aut=False                    => (needs other witness)
n=6 S=[0,2,4] chi(S)={0}  f_is_aut=True   f_expected=False  => unstable witness
n=6 S=[2,4]   chi(S)={0}  f_is_aut=True   f_expected=False  => unstable witness
n=8 S=[0,2,4,6] chi(S)={0} f_is_aut=True f_expected=False   => unstable witness
```

This confirms the precise hypothesis `S ⊆ ker χ` of `cayley_dc_unstable`, and
shows the construction breaks (`f_is_aut=False`) once `S` leaves the kernel —
matching the theoretical analysis.

## 3. OEIS

No single OEIS sequence governs `|Aut(BX)|` across `S`; the orders depend on the
full subset structure rather than only on `|S|`, so no sequence match is
reported. (The stable subsets of `ℤ₄` — count 5 — are too short to fingerprint.)

# Future Directions — Stability of Cayley Digraphs and the `× K₂` Double Cover

Derived from this cycle's findings (`Core.lean`, `Instability.lean`,
`Boundary.lean`, `ComputationalEvidence.md`). The headline discovery is that the
blanket conjecture — *"every even-order abelian Cayley digraph is unstable"* —
is **false** (`Cay(ℤ₄, {0,1})` is stable), while a sharp constructive sufficient
condition (`S` inside a parity-character kernel) is true in full generality.

---

### Conjecture 1 — Parity-kernel characterisation for connected circulants
For a **connected** circulant `Cay(ℤₙ, S)` with `n` even, it is unstable
**iff** there is a surjective homomorphism `χ : ℤₙ → ℤ₂` with `S ⊆ ker χ`
*or* a twin/blow-up obstruction; equivalently the only "elementary" source of
instability is the parity kernel.

*The key insight is...* that in every computed row the parity-kernel witness
`(a,i) ↦ (a, i ⊕ χ a)` already accounts for all *constant-parity* instability,
so the residual unstable mixed-parity cases must come from a structurally
different (twin/quotient) mechanism, which the conjecture isolates.

*Why now?* We already have the kernel direction fully formalized
(`cayley_dc_unstable`) and a decidable stability checker (`Boundary.lean`); the
converse can be attacked one `n` at a time by `native_decide` to build evidence
before a general proof.

---

### Conjecture 2 — Every finite abelian group of even order admits the witness
For **every** finite abelian group `A` of even order there is a surjective
additive homomorphism `χ : A → ℤ₂`; hence `cayley_dc_unstable` applies to *all*
connection sets contained in some index-2 subgroup, not just cyclic ones.

*The key insight is...* that `2 ∣ |A|` forces `A/2A ≠ 0` (equivalently a nonzero
`2`-torsion quotient), and any nonzero elementary-abelian `2`-quotient surjects
onto `ℤ₂`, so the character `χ` of `Instability.lean` always exists.

*Why now?* The cyclic instance is done via `ZMod.castHom`; the general case only
needs the existence lemma `∃ f : A →+ ZMod 2, Surjective f`, a self-contained
group-theory target that immediately upgrades `circulant_dc_unstable` to all
abelian groups.

---

### Conjecture 3 — The "bipartite" twin of the kernel construction
If a surjective `χ : A → ℤ₂` has `S ⊆ A ∖ ker χ` (every generator is *odd*,
the bipartite case), then `Cay(A, S)` is again unstable, witnessed by
translating one connected component of the double cover by a nonzero element of
`ker χ` while fixing the other.

*The key insight is...* that the invariant `J(a,i) = i ⊕ χ(a)` is constant along
arcs when `χ(S) = {1}`, so the double cover splits into two components that can
be moved independently — an automorphism that is provably unexpected whenever
`|ker χ| ≥ 2`.

*Why now?* The computational table shows every all-odd `S` is unstable, and the
component-translation map is as explicit as `chiSwap`; only the
"unexpectedness" bookkeeping remains, mirroring the proof already in
`Instability.lean`.

---

### Conjecture 4 — Stability is `coNP`-flavoured but parity-blind
Deciding stability of `Cay(ℤₙ, S)` is **not** a function of `(n, |S|, χ(S))`
alone: there exist `n` and two sets `S, S'` with the same size and same parity
multiset, one stable and one unstable.

*The key insight is...* that `{0,1,2}` (unstable) and a same-parity-profile
mixed set can already diverge at `n = 4`, so any efficient stability test must
read finer structure (e.g. the Fourier support of `1_S`), not just coarse parity
statistics.

*Why now?* The decidable model in `Core.lean` lets us mine `n ≤ 12` exhaustively
for minimal "parity-twin" pairs, turning the conjecture into a finite search
that can seed an invariant-based classification.

---

### Conjecture 5 — Fourier criterion bridging to additive combinatorics
Instability of `Cay(ℤₙ, S)` (n even) is controlled by the value of the
order-`2` additive character `ψ(x) = stdAddChar(n/2 · x)` on `S`: if `ψ` is
constant on `S` then `Cay(ℤₙ, S)` is unstable.

*The key insight is...* that `ψ(s) = +1 ⟺ s` is even `⟺ χ(s) = false`, so the
parity-kernel hypothesis of `Instability.lean` is *exactly* a statement about a
single Fourier character — directly linking double-cover stability to the
`ZMod.dft` toolkit of `Combinatorics/FourierFiniteGroups.lean`.

*Why now?* Both ingredients already exist in the catalog (the parity character
here, `stdAddChar` and orthogonality there); proving `ψ(s) = 1 ↔ χ(s) = false`
is the one bridge lemma needed to restate all instability results spectrally.

import Mathlib

/-!
# An exact Carathéodory cardinality bound

This file develops the *exact* Carathéodory-type result that underlies the
analysis of contraction bounds in spherical Delaunay refinement (see the
companion file `DelaunayCaratheodory.Refinement`).

The classical Carathéodory theorem states that a point of the convex hull of a
set `s` in a `d`-dimensional real vector space already lies in the convex hull of
an *affinely independent* subset of `s`.  Mathlib provides this as
`convexHull_eq_union`.  What we need downstream, however, is the quantitative
*cardinality* consequence: the representing subset can be taken to have at most
`d + 1` points.  This is the "Carathéodory number" of the space.

## Main results

* `caratheodory_card_bound` : in any finite-dimensional real normed space `E`,
  every point of `convexHull ℝ s` lies in the convex hull of a finite subset of
  `s` of cardinality at most `Module.finrank ℝ E + 1`.
* `caratheodory_card_bound_plane` : the planar specialisation, with the explicit
  bound `3`.
* `caratheodoryNumber` and `caratheodoryNumber_plane` : the abstract Carathéodory
  number `d + 1` of a `d`-dimensional space, and its value `3` in the plane.

## Reference framing

The attached references (`boissonnat2018geometric`, `barber1996quickhull`,
`b-gtfga-80`) all rely on the fact that in `d` dimensions a Delaunay/circumscribed
configuration is controlled by `d + 1` vertices (a simplex).  The cardinality
bound proved here is the convexity counterpart of that combinatorial fact.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): The exact Carathéodory theorem in Mathlib
(`convexHull_eq_union`) can be sharpened to an explicit cardinality bound
`d + 1`, matching the simplex size that governs `d`-dimensional Delaunay
refinement.

Experiment (Experimenter): Unfold `convexHull_eq_union` to extract an affinely
independent representing finset `t`, then apply
`AffineIndependent.card_le_finrank_succ` and bound the `vectorSpan` dimension by
the ambient `finrank` via `Submodule.finrank_le`.  An `omega` closes the
arithmetic.

Analysis (Analyst): The affine-independence in `convexHull_eq_union` is exactly
the data needed; the only nontrivial step is translating `Fintype.card ↥t` to
`t.card` and bounding the span dimension.  No probabilistic / approximate
argument is needed — the result is *exact*.

Critique (Critic): The statement is non-vacuous: it is witnessed by genuine
finsets and the bound is tight (a generic interior point of a `d`-simplex needs
all `d + 1` vertices).  The proof uses real structural lemmas, not `decide`.

Synthesis (PI): This cardinality bound is the reusable convex-geometry core; the
refinement file consumes it to count support points per refinement step.
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

namespace DelaunayCaratheodory

open scoped BigOperators

variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]

/-- The **Carathéodory number** of a `d`-dimensional real space is `d + 1`: the
number of vertices of a `d`-simplex, and the number of points needed to represent
any point of a convex hull. -/
noncomputable def caratheodoryNumber (E : Type*) [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
    [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] : ℕ :=
  Module.finrank ℝ E + 1

/-- **Exact Carathéodory cardinality bound.** Every point in the convex hull of a
set `s` in a finite-dimensional real normed space lies in the convex hull of a
finite subset of `s` of cardinality at most `finrank + 1`. -/
theorem caratheodory_card_bound {s : Set E} {x : E}
    (hx : x ∈ convexHull ℝ s) :
    ∃ t : Finset E, ↑t ⊆ s ∧ t.card ≤ caratheodoryNumber E ∧
      x ∈ convexHull ℝ (↑t : Set E) := by
  rw [convexHull_eq_union] at hx

/-!
# Geometric contraction bounds for iterated refinement

Iterated (spherical) Delaunay refinement repeatedly subdivides a triangulation,
shrinking a scalar quality measure — a circumradius, a longest edge, or a mesh
size — at each step.  Empirically and in the algorithms surveyed by
`boissonnat2018geometric` and `barber1996quickhull` this measure contracts by a
fixed factor `c < 1` per refinement round.  This file isolates the purely
analytic consequences of such a *multiplicative contraction*, independent of any
geometric realisation.

We model the quality measure as a sequence `e : ℕ → ℝ` with `e (n+1) ≤ c * e n`.

## Main results

* `contraction_pow_bound` : `e n ≤ c ^ n * e 0` (geometric decay).
* `contraction_tendsto_zero` : for `c < 1` the measure tends to `0` (the mesh is
  refined to arbitrary fineness).
* `contraction_total_movement` : for `c < 1` the measure is summable and the
  *total work* satisfies `∑' n, e n ≤ e 0 / (1 - c)`.
* `contraction_total_sharp` : the bound is **sharp** — the geometric sequence
  `e n = c ^ n * r` attains it with equality.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): A per-step multiplicative contraction `e(n+1) ≤ c·e(n)`
with `0 ≤ c < 1` forces (i) geometric decay, (ii) convergence to `0`, and
(iii) a *finite, explicitly bounded* total accumulated movement
`∑ e n ≤ e 0/(1-c)`, and this last bound is sharp.

Experiment (Experimenter): (i) by induction with `mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left`;
(ii) `squeeze_zero` against `c^n · e 0 → 0`
(`tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_lt_one`); (iii) dominate `e` by the geometric
series `c^n · e 0` and evaluate via `tsum_geometric_of_lt_one`; sharpness by
exhibiting the geometric sequence and computing its `tsum` directly.

Analysis (Analyst): Nonnegativity `0 ≤ e n` is needed only for summability and
the limit (to apply `squeeze_zero` / `Summable.of_nonneg_of_le`); the pure decay
bound holds without it.  The sharpness witness shows `e 0/(1-c)` cannot be
improved, so the "total refinement work" estimate is tight, not merely an upper
bound.

Critique (Critic): The hypotheses are minimal (`0 ≤ c`, and `c < 1` only where
genuinely required).  No hypothesis is vacuous; each main theorem uses a real
inductive / analytic argument rather than `decide` or `simp` alone.

Synthesis (PI): These contraction estimates are the analytic half of the
refinement story; combined with the Carathéodory cardinality bound they yield the
refinement-convergence theorem in `DelaunayCaratheodory.Refinement`.
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-/

namespace DelaunayCaratheodory

open scoped BigOperators Topology

/-- **Geometric decay.** If a nonnegative quality measure contracts by factor
`c ≥ 0` each step, it is bounded by `c ^ n * e 0` after `n` steps. -/
theorem contraction_pow_bound (e : ℕ → ℝ) (c : ℝ) (hc : 0 ≤ c)
    (hstep : ∀ n, e (n + 1) ≤ c * e n) :
    ∀ n, e n ≤ c ^ n * e 0 := by
  intro n
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
    calc e (k + 1) ≤ c * e k := hstep k
      _ ≤ c * (c ^ k * e 0) := mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ih hc
      _ = c ^ (k + 1) * e 0 := by ring

/-- **Refinement to arbitrary fineness.** With contraction factor `c < 1`, the
quality measure tends to `0`. -/
theorem contraction_tendsto_zero (e : ℕ → ℝ) (c : ℝ) (hc : 0 ≤ c) (hc1 : c < 1)
    (he : ∀ n, 0 ≤ e n) (hstep : ∀ n, e (n + 1) ≤ c * e n) :
    Filter.Tendsto e Filter.atTop (𝓝 0) := by
  have hb := contraction_pow_bound e c hc hstep
  apply squeeze_zero he hb
  simpa using (tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_lt_one hc hc1).mul_const (e 0)

/-- **Bounded total work.** With contraction factor `c < 1`, the quality measure
is summable and the total accumulated movement is at most `e 0 / (1 - c)`. -/
theorem contraction_total_movement (e : ℕ → ℝ) (c : ℝ) (hc : 0 ≤ c) (hc1 : c < 1)
    (he : ∀ n, 0 ≤ e n) (hstep : ∀ n, e (n + 1) ≤ c * e n) :
    Summable e ∧ ∑' n, e n ≤ e 0 / (1 - c) := by
  have hb := contraction_pow_bound e c hc hstep
  have hsummable_geo : Summable (fun n => c ^ n * e 0) :=
    (summable_geometric_of_lt_one hc hc1).mul_right _
  have hsum : Summable e := Summable.of_nonneg_of_le he hb hsummable_geo
  refine ⟨hsum, ?_⟩
  calc ∑' n, e n ≤ ∑' n, c ^ n * e 0 := hsum.tsum_mono hsummable_geo hb
    _ = (∑' n, c ^ n) * e 0 := by rw [tsum_mul_right]
    _ = (1 - c)⁻¹ * e 0 := by rw [tsum_geometric_of_lt_one hc hc1]
    _ = e 0 / (1 - c) := by rw [div_eq_inv_mul]

/-- **Sharpness.** The geometric sequence `e n = c ^ n * r` exactly contracts by
`c` each step and attains the total-work bound `r / (1 - c)` with equality, so the
estimate in `contraction_total_movement` cannot be improved. -/
theorem contraction_total_sharp (c r : ℝ) (hc : 0 ≤ c) (hc1 : c < 1) :
    let e := fun n => c ^ n * r
    (∀ n, e (n + 1) = c * e n) ∧ ∑' n, e n = r / (1 - c) := by
  intro e
  refine ⟨fun n => by show c ^ (n + 1) * r = c * (c ^ n * r); ring, ?_⟩
  show ∑' n, c ^ n * r = r / (1 - c)
  rw [tsum_mul_right, tsum_geometric_of_lt_one hc hc1, div_eq_inv_mul]

end DelaunayCaratheodory

model of *iterated spherical Delaunay refinement* and its convergence theorem.

A refinement maintains a finite-dimensional ambient space `E`, a (scalar) radius /
mesh-quality measure `radius n` that contracts by a fixed factor `factor < 1`, and
— at every stage — inserts new points into the convex hull of the current active
vertex set.  The contraction half (`DelaunayCaratheodory.Contraction`) controls
the *speed* of refinement; the Carathéodory half
(`DelaunayCaratheodory.Caratheodory`) controls the *combinatorial width* of each
step, bounding the number of vertices supporting any inserted point by the
Carathéodory number `d + 1`.

## Main results

* `SphericalRefinement` : the data of a contracting refinement.
* `SphericalRefinement.radius_geometric` : geometric decay of the mesh measure.
* `SphericalRefinement.radius_tendsto_zero` : the mesh is refined to fineness `0`.
* `SphericalRefinement.total_radius_bound` : total refinement work is finite and
  `≤ radius 0 / (1 - factor)`.
* `SphericalRefinement.support_card_bound` : every inserted point is supported by
  at most `caratheodoryNumber E = d + 1` active vertices.
* `SphericalRefinement.refinement_convergence` : the combined statement — fineness
  to `0`, bounded total work, and bounded per-step support — the contraction
  analysis "using an exact Carathéodory-type result".

Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): A spherical Delaunay refinement whose mesh measure
contracts geometrically converges to a zero-fineness limit with *finite total
work*, while every inserted circumcenter remains supported by at most `d + 1`
active vertices.  The two phenomena (analytic decay, combinatorial width) are
genuinely independent and combine into one convergence theorem.

specialise `contraction_pow_bound`, `contraction_tendsto_zero`,
`contraction_total_movement`; bound the support of an inserted point via
`caratheodory_card_bound`.  Package all three into `refinement_convergence`.

Analysis (Analyst): The Carathéodory bound is *exact* (`d + 1`) and dimension-
driven, whereas the contraction bound is *metric* and factor-driven.  No
hypothesis links them, which is precisely why the combined theorem is informative:
fineness and width are controlled by orthogonal data.

Critique (Critic): The structure's hypotheses are non-vacuous (a constant-`0`
radius with any `factor ∈ [0,1)` is a witness, as is a genuine geometric decay).
The convergence theorem is not vacuously true: it delivers an explicit finite
bound and an explicit support cardinality.  Both halves use real lemmas.

Synthesis (PI): `refinement_convergence` is the headline result of the cycle:
contraction speed and Carathéodory width are simultaneously controlled, matching
the simplex-driven picture in `boissonnat2018geometric` / `barber1996quickhull`.

namespace DelaunayCaratheodory

open scoped BigOperators Topology

/-- The data of an **iterated spherical Delaunay refinement**: a scalar mesh
quality measure `radius` that contracts by a fixed `factor < 1` at every step. -/
structure SphericalRefinement (E : Type*) [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
    [FiniteDimensional ℝ E] where
  /-- The mesh quality measure (e.g. maximal circumradius) after `n` refinements. -/
  radius : ℕ → ℝ
  /-- The per-step contraction factor. -/
  factor : ℝ
  /-- The mesh measure is nonnegative. -/
  radius_nonneg : ∀ n, 0 ≤ radius n
  /-- The contraction factor is nonnegative. -/
  factor_nonneg : 0 ≤ factor
  /-- The refinement is a genuine contraction. -/
  factor_lt_one : factor < 1
  /-- Each refinement step contracts the mesh measure. -/
  contracts : ∀ n, radius (n + 1) ≤ factor * radius n

namespace SphericalRefinement

variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]
variable (R : SphericalRefinement E)

/-- Geometric decay of the mesh measure. -/
theorem radius_geometric (n : ℕ) : R.radius n ≤ R.factor ^ n * R.radius 0 :=
  contraction_pow_bound R.radius R.factor R.factor_nonneg R.contracts n

/-- The mesh is refined to arbitrary fineness: `radius n → 0`. -/
theorem radius_tendsto_zero :
    Filter.Tendsto R.radius Filter.atTop (𝓝 0) :=
  contraction_tendsto_zero R.radius R.factor R.factor_nonneg R.factor_lt_one
    R.radius_nonneg R.contracts

/-- Total refinement work is finite and bounded by `radius 0 / (1 - factor)`. -/
theorem total_radius_bound :
    Summable R.radius ∧ ∑' n, R.radius n ≤ R.radius 0 / (1 - R.factor) :=
  contraction_total_movement R.radius R.factor R.factor_nonneg R.factor_lt_one
    R.radius_nonneg R.contracts

/-- **Carathéodory width.** Any point inserted into the convex hull of the active
vertex set `s` is supported by at most `caratheodoryNumber E = d + 1` of those
vertices. -/
theorem support_card_bound {s : Set E} {x : E} (hx : x ∈ convexHull ℝ s) :
    ∃ t : Finset E, ↑t ⊆ s ∧ t.card ≤ caratheodoryNumber E ∧
      x ∈ convexHull ℝ (↑t : Set E) :=
  caratheodory_card_bound hx

/-- **Refinement convergence.** The combined statement: the mesh measure tends to
`0` (refinement to arbitrary fineness), the total accumulated work is finite and
explicitly bounded, and every inserted point is supported by at most `d + 1`
active vertices. This is the contraction analysis "using an exact
Carathéodory-type result". -/
theorem refinement_convergence {s : Set E} {x : E} (hx : x ∈ convexHull ℝ s) :
    Filter.Tendsto R.radius Filter.atTop (𝓝 0) ∧
    (Summable R.radius ∧ ∑' n, R.radius n ≤ R.radius 0 / (1 - R.factor)) ∧
    (∃ t : Finset E, ↑t ⊆ s ∧ t.card ≤ caratheodoryNumber E ∧
      x ∈ convexHull ℝ (↑t : Set E)) :=
  ⟨R.radius_tendsto_zero, R.total_radius_bound, support_card_bound hx⟩

end SphericalRefinement

end DelaunayCaratheodory

## Conjecture 1 — Maurey/approximate Carathéodory with explicit rate

In a real inner-product space, for `x` in the convex hull of points of norm `≤ 1`,
there is an average of `k` of them within `ℓ²`-distance `≤ 1/√k` of `x`, and `1/√k`
is optimal in the worst case.

*The key insight is* that the *exact* cardinality bound `d + 1` proved here is a
dimension-driven ceiling, whereas the *approximate* count `k ≈ 1/ε²` is
dimension-free — so the two regimes should be unified by a single
variance-identity `E‖avg − x‖² = (Σλᵢ‖vᵢ‖² − ‖x‖²)/k`.

*Why now?* The exact bound and its sharpness witness (simplex centroid) are now
formal; the approximate version reduces to formalizing one finite expectation
identity over `(Fin m)^k`, which the present convexity scaffolding makes reachable.

## Conjecture 2 — Dimension-dependent contraction factor for Delaunay refinement

For a genuine spherical Delaunay refinement in `ℝ^d`, the worst-case per-step
circumradius contraction factor is bounded away from `1` by a quantity depending
only on `d` (and not on the input), so `factor ≤ 1 − c_d` for an explicit `c_d`.

*The key insight is* that each refinement step replaces a circumcenter that, by the
Carathéodory width bound, is supported by exactly `d + 1` vertices, giving a finite
combinatorial menu of "shapes" whose contraction can be bounded uniformly.

*Why now?* `SphericalRefinement` already abstracts the contraction factor as a free
parameter; pinning `factor` to a dimensional constant turns the abstract
convergence theorem into a fully quantitative algorithmic guarantee.

## Conjecture 3 — Total work is Θ(log(1/ε)) refinement rounds for fineness ε

Reaching mesh fineness `ε` requires `Θ(log(1/ε) / log(1/factor))` rounds, and the
constant is sharp; the bounded-total-work estimate `e₀/(1−factor)` is the integral
of this logarithmic profile.

*The key insight is* that geometric decay `e n ≤ factor^n e₀` (proved) inverts to a
logarithmic round count, and the sharpness sequence shows the inversion is tight.

*Why now?* `contraction_pow_bound` and `contraction_total_sharp` give both the upper
bound and its matching witness; only the explicit round-count inversion remains.

## Conjecture 4 — Carathéodory width controls per-step update cost

In any incremental convex-hull / Delaunay algorithm, the amortized number of
hull facets touched per inserted point is `O(d)` precisely because every inserted
point is supported by at most `d + 1` prior vertices.

*The key insight is* that `support_card_bound` converts a geometric insertion into a
bounded-support combinatorial event, decoupling update cost from the current hull
size.

*Why now?* The width bound is formal and dimension-exact; linking it to a counting
model of facet updates is the natural next combinatorial step.

## Conjecture 5 — Sharpness transfers to ℓ^p Carathéodory numbers

For `ℓ^p` balls the relevant "approximate Carathéodory number" scales like
`p · R² / ε²`, and the `d + 1` exact bound is recovered as `ε → 0`, exhibiting a
continuous interpolation between the exact and approximate regimes.

*The key insight is* that the exact bound is the `ε → 0` limit of the approximate
one, so both should be corollaries of a single parametric inequality in `(p, ε, d)`.

*Why now?* With the exact endpoint formalized, only the `p`-dependent variance
estimate is missing to interpolate the whole family.

    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_powerset] at hA
    simp only [Finset.mem_powerset]
    exact Finset.sdiff_subset_sdiff hA.1 (le_refl S)
  · intro A hA B hB heq
    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_powerset] at hA hB
    have : (A \ S) ∪ S = (B \ S) ∪ S := by rw [heq]
    rwa [Finset.sdiff_union_of_subset hA.2, Finset.sdiff_union_of_subset hB.2] at this
  · intro B hB
    simp only [Finset.mem_powerset] at hB
    refine ⟨B ∪ S, ?_, ?_⟩
    · simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_powerset]
      refine ⟨Finset.union_subset (hB.trans (Finset.sdiff_subset)) h, Finset.subset_union_right⟩
    · rw [Finset.union_sdiff_right]
      apply Finset.sdiff_eq_self_of_disjoint
      exact (Finset.disjoint_left.2 (fun x hxB hxS => ((Finset.mem_sdiff.1 (hB hxB)).2) hxS))

/-- The number of subsets of `Gr` disjoint from a fixed `S ⊆ Gr` is also
`2 ^ (|Gr| − |S|)` (complement involution `A ↦ Gr \ A`). -/
lemma card_filter_disjoint {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α] (Gr S : Finset α) (h : S ⊆ Gr) :
    (Gr.powerset.filter (fun A => Disjoint S A)).card = 2 ^ (Gr.card - S.card) := by
  rw [← card_filter_superset Gr S h]
  apply Finset.card_bij (fun A _ => Gr \ A)
  · intro A hA
    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_powerset] at hA ⊢
    refine ⟨Finset.sdiff_subset, ?_⟩
    intro x hxS
    rw [Finset.mem_sdiff]
    exact ⟨h hxS, fun hxA => (Finset.disjoint_left.1 hA.2) hxS hxA⟩
  · intro A hA B hB heq
    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_powerset] at hA hB
    have : Gr \ (Gr \ A) = Gr \ (Gr \ B) := by rw [heq]
    rwa [Finset.sdiff_sdiff_eq_self hA.1, Finset.sdiff_sdiff_eq_self hB.1] at this
  · intro B hB
    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_powerset] at hB
    refine ⟨Gr \ B, ?_, ?_⟩
    · simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_powerset]
      refine ⟨Finset.sdiff_subset, ?_⟩
      rw [Finset.disjoint_right]
      intro x hx
      rw [Finset.mem_sdiff] at hx
      exact fun hxS => hx.2 (hB.2 hxS)
    · rw [Finset.sdiff_sdiff_eq_self hB.1]

/-! ## The union bound: existence of a good colouring -/

/-
**Probabilistic existence.** If `k ≤ n` and `2 · C(n,k) < 2^{C(k,2)}`, then
there is a red edge set `R` (a 2-colouring of `K_n`) with no monochromatic
`K_k`: no `k`-set has all its edges red, and no `k`-set has all its edges blue.
-/
lemma exists_good_coloring (hkn : k ≤ n) (hlt : 2 * n.choose k < 2 ^ (k.choose 2)) :
    ∃ R : Finset (Sym2 (Fin n)),
      (∀ T : Finset (Fin n), T.card = k → ¬ edgesOn T ⊆ R) ∧
      (∀ T : Finset (Fin n), T.card = k → ¬ Disjoint (edgesOn T) R) := by
  -- By the union bound, the number of colorings where some k-element subset is monochromatic is strictly less than the total number of colorings.
  have h_union_bound : (∑ T ∈ Finset.powersetCard k (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)), ((Finset.powerset (edgesOn (univ : Finset (Fin n)))).filter (fun R => edgesOn T ⊆ R)).card + ∑ T ∈ Finset.powersetCard k (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)), ((Finset.powerset (edgesOn (univ : Finset (Fin n)))).filter (fun R => Disjoint (edgesOn T) R)).card) < 2 ^ (n.choose 2) := by
    -- By the properties of binomial coefficients and the union bound, we can show that the sum of the cardinalities of the sets of red and blue colorings is less than $2^{n \choose 2}$.
    have h_sum : ∑ T ∈ Finset.powersetCard k (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)), (2 ^ (n.choose 2 - k.choose 2) + 2 ^ (n.choose 2 - k.choose 2)) < 2 ^ (n.choose 2) := by
      simp_all +decide [ ← two_mul, Finset.card_univ ];
      rw [ show 2 ^ n.choose 2 = 2 ^ ( n.choose 2 - k.choose 2 ) * 2 ^ k.choose 2 by rw [ ← pow_add, Nat.sub_add_cancel ( show k.choose 2 ≤ n.choose 2 from Nat.choose_le_choose _ hkn ) ] ] ; nlinarith [ pow_pos ( zero_lt_two' ℕ ) ( n.choose 2 - k.choose 2 ) ] ;
    convert h_sum using 1;
    rw [ ← Finset.sum_add_distrib, Finset.sum_congr rfl ];
    intro T hT; rw [ card_filter_superset, card_filter_disjoint ] <;> norm_num [ Finset.mem_powersetCard.mp hT, card_edgesOn ] ;
    · exact edgesOn_subset_univ T;
    · exact edgesOn_subset_univ T;
  contrapose! h_union_bound;
  have h_union_bound : Finset.powerset (edgesOn (univ : Finset (Fin n))) ⊆ Finset.biUnion (Finset.powersetCard k (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n))) (fun T => (Finset.powerset (edgesOn (univ : Finset (Fin n)))).filter (fun R => edgesOn T ⊆ R) ∪ (Finset.powerset (edgesOn (univ : Finset (Fin n)))).filter (fun R => Disjoint (edgesOn T) R)) := by
    intro R hR; specialize h_union_bound R; by_cases h : ∃ T : Finset ( Fin n ), #T = k ∧ edgesOn T ⊆ R <;> aesop;
  refine' le_trans _ ( Finset.card_mono h_union_bound ) |> le_trans <| _;
  · rw [ Finset.card_powerset, card_edgesOn_univ ];
  · exact le_trans ( Finset.card_biUnion_le ) ( by rw [ ← Finset.sum_add_distrib ] ; exact Finset.sum_le_sum fun _ _ => Finset.card_union_le _ _ )

/-! ## The probabilistic lower bound -/

/-
**Erdős probabilistic lower bound.** If `k ≤ n` and `2 · C(n,k) < 2^{C(k,2)}`,
then `K_n` has a 2-colouring with no monochromatic `K_k`, i.e. `R(k,k) > n`.
-/
theorem not_arrows_of_counting (hkn : k ≤ n) (hlt : 2 * n.choose k < 2 ^ (k.choose 2)) :
    ¬ Arrows n k k := by
  intro h;
  obtain ⟨R, hR⟩ := exists_good_coloring hkn hlt;
  specialize h ( graphOf R ) Finset.univ;
  simp_all +decide [ Finset.card_univ ];
  rcases h with ( ⟨ S, hS ⟩ | ⟨ S, hS ⟩ ) <;> have := isNClique_graphOf_iff R k S <;> have := isNClique_compl_graphOf_iff R k S <;> simp_all +decide [ SimpleGraph.isNClique_iff, SimpleGraph.isNIndepSet_iff ]

/-
**Clean exponential corollary.** Using the crude bound `C(n,k) ≤ n^k`, any `n`
with `2 · n^k < 2^{C(k,2)}` (and `k ≤ n`) satisfies `R(k,k) > n`.
-/
theorem not_arrows_of_pow (hkn : k ≤ n) (hlt : 2 * n ^ k < 2 ^ (k.choose 2)) :
    ¬ Arrows n k k := by
  exact not_arrows_of_counting hkn ( by linarith [ Nat.choose_le_pow n k ] )

/-
**Concrete exponential lower bound:** `R(10,10) > 16`.  (Here `2·16^10 = 2^41
< 2^45 = 2^{C(10,2)}`, so a random 2-colouring of `K₁₆` is `K₁₀`-free in both
colours with positive probability.)
-/
theorem ramsey_ten_lower : ¬ Arrows 16 10 10 :=
  not_arrows_of_pow (by norm_num) (by norm_num [Nat.choose_two_right])

/- -- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
ANALYSIS (Analyst): what survived and why.
* SURVIVED: the full finite double-count.  The two structural pillars are
  `card_filter_superset` (interval cardinality `#[S, Gr] = 2^(|Gr|-|S|)`) and its
  blue mirror `card_filter_disjoint`, obtained from the *same* lemma through the
  complement involution `A ↦ Gr \ A`.  This symmetry is exactly the
  red/blue symmetry of the colouring, made cardinal.
* NEEDED A DIFFERENT DEFINITION: encoding a colouring as a `SimpleGraph` and
  counting `Fintype.card (SimpleGraph (Fin n))` directly is painful.  Switching
  to the *red edge set* model `R ⊆ edgesOn univ` (a `Finset (Sym2 (Fin n))`) made
  the counting a plain `Finset.powerset` computation, with `graphOf` and the two
  `isNClique_*_iff` bridge lemmas translating back to the `Arrows` framework.
* TRUE BUT WEAK AT SMALL k: for `k = 3` the bound only yields `¬ Arrows 3 3 3`
  (since `C(4,3)=4` is not `< 4 = 2^{C(3,2)}/2`), far from the true `R(3,3)=6`.
  The probabilistic method is an *asymptotic* tool; sharpness at small `k`
  belongs to the structural files (`RamseyThreeFour`, `RamseyFourFour`).  This is
  not a defect — it is the qualitative divide between the two halves of Ramsey
  theory.

CRITIQUE (Critic): adversarial review.
* Triviality?  No: the main theorem is a genuine union bound with an exponent
  manipulation `2^{C(n,2)} = 2^{C(k,2)} · 2^{C(n,2)-C(k,2)}`; it is not `decide`,
  not definitional, and not vacuous (`ramsey_ten_lower` exhibits a real instance
  `R(10,10) > 16`).
* Hidden vacuity?  `not_arrows_of_counting` is applied to a nonempty hypothesis
  family: `exists_good_coloring` actually *produces* the avoiding colouring `R`,
  so the negation `¬ Arrows` is witnessed, not vacuous.
* Boundary `k > n` (Extra Adversarial Mandate counterexample): the statement
  `¬ Arrows n k k` stays true there, but the proof's exponent split requires
  `C(k,2) ≤ C(n,2)`, i.e. `k ≤ n`.  We therefore keep `k ≤ n` as an explicit,
  load-bearing hypothesis of the *proof*; it always holds in the lower-bound
  regime (`n` large), so nothing of value is lost.

SYNTHESIS (Principal Investigator): the diagonal Ramsey number obeys two
independent laws.  STRUCTURE pins the small exact values; COUNTING forces the
exponential growth `R(k,k) > 2^{(k-?)/2}`.  This file supplies the second law in
the same `Arrows` vocabulary as the first, so both live in one framework:
`not_arrows_of_counting` (general), `not_arrows_of_pow` (clean exponential
corollary via `C(n,k) ≤ n^k`), and `ramsey_ten_lower` (a concrete witness).
-/

end RamseyTheory

# Computational Evidence — Probabilistic lower bounds for diagonal Ramsey numbers

All numbers below were produced with `#eval` in Lean (kernel-evaluated `Nat`
arithmetic), so they are exact, not floating-point estimates.

## 1. The counting threshold

For the two-colour diagonal Ramsey number `R(k,k)`, the Erdős first-moment
argument gives `R(k,k) > n` whenever `2·C(n,k) < 2^{C(k,2)}`.  Using the crude
slack `C(n,k) ≤ n^k` weakens the test to `2·n^k < 2^{C(k,2)}`.

For each `k`, let
* `best(k)`   = largest `n` with `2·C(n,k) < 2^{C(k,2)}`  (sharp counting bound),
* `bestpow(k)`= largest `n` with `2·n^k   < 2^{C(k,2)}`  (crude `n^k` bound).

| k  | best(k) = R(k,k) > | bestpow(k) = R(k,k) > |
|----|--------------------|------------------------|
| 2  | 1                  | 0                      |
| 3  | 3                  | 1                      |
| 4  | 6                  | 2                      |
| 5  | 11                 | 3                      |
| 6  | 17                 | 5                      |
| 7  | 27                 | 7                      |
| 8  | 42                 | 10                     |
| 9  | 65                 | 14                     |
| 10 | 100                | 21                     |
| 11 | 152                | 30                     |
| 12 | 231                | 42                     |
| 13 | 349                | 60                     |

Both columns grow exponentially (`best(k) ≈ 2^{k/2}·k!^{-1/?}`,
`bestpow(k) ≈ 2^{k/2}`).  The gap between the two columns is exactly the `k!`
factor discarded by `C(n,k) ≤ n^k`.

The formal `ramsey_ten_lower : ¬ Arrows 16 10 10` (i.e. `R(10,10) > 16`) is a
*conservative* instance of the crude `bestpow(10) = 21` row, chosen so the
exponent arithmetic `2·16^10 = 2^41 < 2^45 = 2^{C(10,2)}` is a clean power-of-two
comparison.

## 2. The even-diagonal family

`ramsey_lower_even` instantiates `k = 2m`, `n = 2^{m-1}`.  The table confirms the
side conditions and that `2^{m-1}` stays below the (larger) sharp threshold:

| m | k = 2m | n = 2^{m-1} (our bound) | best(2m) (sharp) |
|---|--------|--------------------------|-------------------|
| 4 | 8      | 8                        | 42                |
| 5 | 10     | 16                       | 100               |
| 6 | 12     | 32                       | 231               |
| 7 | 14     | 64                       | 527               |
| 8 | 16     | 128                      | 1186              |

So `2^{m-1} ≤ best(2m)` throughout (our crude family bound is valid and
conservative), and `2m ≤ 2^{m-1}` holds from `m = 4` on (`8 ≤ 8`, `10 ≤ 16`, …),
matching the `m ≥ 4` hypothesis of `ramsey_lower_even`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt (Extra Adversarial Mandate)

* **`m = 3` boundary.**  `2m = 6` but `2^{m-1} = 4`, so the side condition
  `2m ≤ n` fails (`6 ≤ 4` is false).  Hence the lower bound is *not* claimed at
  `m = 3`; the `m ≥ 4` hypothesis is the exact boundary, not a convenience.
* **Small-`k` weakness.**  At `k = 3` the counting test only certifies
  `R(3,3) > 3`, far from the true `R(3,3) = 6` (proved structurally elsewhere in
  the catalog).  No counterexample to the *theorem* exists — the method is simply
  asymptotic, confirming the "two laws" analysis in the Lab Notes.

## 4. Known exact values (sanity anchor)

The exact diagonal values currently known are `R(1,1)=1`, `R(2,2)=2`,
`R(3,3)=6`, `R(4,4)=18` (and no further `R(k,k)` is known exactly).  Every row of
the `best(k)` column above is strictly below the corresponding known/true value
where comparison is possible (`best(3)=3 < 6`, `best(4)=6 < 18`), as a lower
bound must be.

# Future Directions — Probabilistic Ramsey lower bounds

Derived from this cycle's findings (see the Lab Notes in
`RamseyProbabilisticLowerBound.lean` and `RamseyDiagonalSandwich.lean`).  This
cycle formalised, on the catalog's shared `Arrows` framework:

* `not_arrows_of_counting` — the Erdős first-moment lower bound
  `2·C(n,k) < 2^{C(k,2)} → R(k,k) > n`;
* `not_arrows_of_pow` — its clean `C(n,k) ≤ n^k` corollary;
* `ramsey_lower_even` / `ramsey_even_sandwich` — an explicit infinite family
  `2^{m-1} < R(2m,2m) ≤ 4^{2m-1}`.

The findings below are bold, falsifiable next steps.

## 1. Replace `n^k` by `n^k / k!` to reach the true base `√2`.
**Conjecture.** `not_arrows_of_counting` can be upgraded to a fully general
`∀ k ≥ 3, ¬ Arrows ⌊2^{k/2}⌋ k k`, recovering the textbook `R(k,k) > 2^{k/2}`.
**The key insight is...** the only slack between our `bestpow(k)` column and the
sharp `best(k)` column in `ComputationalEvidence.md` is the single factor `k!`
dropped by `C(n,k) ≤ n^k`; reinstating `C(n,k) ≤ n^k/k!` (provable from
`Nat.choose_le_pow_div_factorial`-style bounds) closes the entire gap.
**Why now?** The counting core (`card_filter_superset`, `exists_good_coloring`)
is already proved and base-free; only one arithmetic inequality stands between
the present `2^{k/2-1}` family and the optimal `2^{k/2}` constant.

## 2. Lovász Local Lemma improves the constant to `√2·k/e`.
**Conjecture.** A symmetric-LLL refinement yields
`R(k,k) > (1+o(1))·(k/(e√2))·2^{k/2}`, strictly beating the first-moment bound,
and is formalisable as `¬ Arrows n k k` under a dependency-degree hypothesis.
**The key insight is...** the "bad events" indexed by `k`-sets `T` in
`exists_good_coloring` are *almost* independent — two events interact only when
their vertex sets share an edge — so the union bound is wasteful exactly where
the LLL is sharp.
**Why now?** Our bad events are already explicit `Finset`s
(`Gr.powerset.filter (edgesOn T ⊆ ·)`); their pairwise dependency graph is
combinatorially concrete, making a finite LLL instance directly expressible.

## 3. The off-diagonal bound `R(3,k) = Θ(k²/log k)`.
**Conjecture.** The same edge-set counting model proves the off-diagonal lower
bound `R(3,k) > c·(k/log k)^2` (Kim's order of magnitude), via a triangle-free
process / alteration argument stated as `¬ Arrows n 3 k`.
**The key insight is...** for `s = 3` the "red" bad events are triangles, a
*sparse* structure, so deleting one vertex per monochromatic triangle (the
alteration method) costs far less than the first-moment union bound.
**Why now?** `not_arrows_of_counting` already separates the red (`edgesOn T ⊆ R`)
and blue (`Disjoint (edgesOn T) R`) events asymmetrically, so an asymmetric
`s = 3`, `t = k` specialisation is a natural and immediate generalisation.

## 4. A constructive (derandomised) witness colouring.
**Conjecture.** The existence proof in `exists_good_coloring` can be made
*constructive*: the method of conditional expectations selects, edge by edge, an
explicit `R : Finset (Sym2 (Fin n))` realising `¬ Arrows n k k`, computable by
`decide`/`native_decide` for moderate `n, k`.
**The key insight is...** our bound is a strict inequality of exact `Nat`
cardinalities (`bad.card < Gr.powerset.card`), so the averaging argument already
pinpoints a non-empty `Gr.powerset \ bad`; greedily fixing each edge to keep the
conditional count below threshold extracts a concrete element.
**Why now?** Every quantity in the proof is a decidable `Finset.card`, so the
derandomisation is a finite search with a proven-correct pruning bound.

## 5. Tightening the sandwich exponent gap.
**Conjecture.** `ramsey_even_sandwich`'s gap can be narrowed from
`[2^{m-1}, 4^{2m-1}] = [2^{(k/2)-1}, 2^{2k-2}]` to `[2^{k/2}, 2^{2k}]`, and the
upper exponent reduced via the Conlon/Sah polynomial improvement to `R(k,k) ≤
4^{k}·k^{-c log k}`.
**The key insight is...** the lower and upper bounds are proved by *disjoint*
mechanisms (counting vs. recursion) sharing only the `Arrows` vocabulary, so each
exponent can be improved independently without touching the other.
**Why now?** Both endpoints are already theorems in this catalog on one
framework; closing the base-of-exponent gap `[√2, 4]` is the central open problem
of the field, and a formal sandwich is the natural scaffold for incremental
progress.

This file develops a rigorous, fully-proved fragment of the *finite-field model*
of the Kakeya problem.  The full Kakeya conjecture (a Besicovitch set in `ℝ^n`

The "bad" set removed from the full plane: off-origin points of the vertical
axis `{(0, b) : b ≠ 0}`, which has `q − 1` points.
-/
theorem bad_card :
    (Finset.univ.filter (fun p : F × F => p.1 = 0 ∧ p ≠ (0, 0))).card
      = Fintype.card F - 1 := by
  rw [ Finset.card_eq_sum_ones ];
  rw [ show ( Finset.filter ( fun x : F × F => x.1 = 0 ∧ ¬x = ( 0, 0 ) ) Finset.univ : Finset ( F × F ) ) = Finset.image ( fun x : F => ( 0, x ) ) ( Finset.univ.erase 0 ) from ?_, Finset.sum_image ] <;> norm_num;
  grind

/-
**Bush count.** The bush of lines through the origin in `F²` has exactly
`q² − q + 1` points, where `q = |F|`.
-/
theorem bush_card :
    (bush F).card = Fintype.card F * Fintype.card F - Fintype.card F + 1 := by
  rw [ bush_eq, tsub_add_eq_add_tsub ];
  · convert Finset.card_univ_diff ( Finset.univ.filter fun p : F × F => p.1 = 0 ∧ p ≠ ( 0, 0 ) ) using 1;
    · exact congr_arg _ ( by ext; by_cases h : ‹F × F›.1 = 0 <;> by_cases h' : ‹F × F› = ( 0, 0 ) <;> simp +decide [ h, h' ] );
    · rw [ Fintype.card_prod, bad_card ];
      rw [ Nat.sub_eq_of_eq_add ];
      linarith [ Nat.sub_add_cancel ( show 1 ≤ Fintype.card F from Fintype.card_pos ), Nat.sub_add_cancel ( show Fintype.card F - 1 ≤ Fintype.card F * Fintype.card F from Nat.sub_le_of_le_add <| by nlinarith ) ];
  · nlinarith

/-- **Incidence lemma.** Two lines through the origin of distinct slopes meet only
at the origin. -/
theorem line_distinct_slope_inter {m₁ m₂ : F} (h : m₁ ≠ m₂) :
    line m₁ ∩ line m₂ = {(0, 0)} := by
  ext p
  simp only [line, mem_inter, mem_image, mem_univ, true_and, mem_singleton]
  constructor <;> intro hp <;> aesop

/-- A *Kakeya set* in the through-origin model: a set containing a full line of
every slope through the origin. -/
def IsKakeyaSet (K : Finset (F × F)) : Prop := ∀ m : F, line m ⊆ K

/-- **Kakeya lower bound (finite-field, through-origin model).** Any Kakeya set in
`F²` has at least `q² − q + 1` points: it must contain the whole bush. -/
theorem card_ge_of_isKakeyaSet {K : Finset (F × F)} (hK : IsKakeyaSet K) :
    Fintype.card F * Fintype.card F - Fintype.card F + 1 ≤ K.card := by
  rw [← bush_card]
  exact Finset.card_le_card (Finset.biUnion_subset.mpr fun m _ => hK m)

end KakeyaBush

import Mathlib

/-!
# The additive-combinatorics bridge: sumset growth (Katz–Tao framework)

The Katz–Tao approach to the Kakeya problem reduces dimension lower bounds to
*sum–difference* estimates in additive combinatorics: a Kakeya set forces a
configuration whose iterated sumsets must grow, and quantitative growth
translates back into a dimension bound.  The cleanest exactly-provable engine of
this kind is the **Cauchy–Davenport** inequality in the prime cyclic group
`ZMod p`.

This file proves the iterated-sumset growth law that powers such arguments:

  `|kA| ≥ min(p, k·(|A| − 1) + 1)`  for every nonempty `A ⊆ ZMod p`,

by induction on `k` using Cauchy–Davenport, and deduces the qualitative
corollary that any set with at least two elements *generates the whole group*
under enough additions (`kA = ZMod p` once `k ≥ p − 1`).  This is the discrete
analogue of "a Kakeya set, after enough additive combination, fills space".

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
* Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): Cauchy–Davenport should iterate to a linear-in-`k`
  growth `|kA| ≳ k|A|` until saturation at `p`.  Predicted exact bound
  `min(p, k(|A|−1)+1)`.
* Experiment (Experimenter): defined `sumIter A k` by recursion (`A + (A + …)`),
  proved nonemptiness by induction, and ran the induction on `k`, feeding
  `ZMod.cauchy_davenport` at each step.  The `min` and `ℕ`-subtraction bookkeeping
  was the only real obstacle (handled with `omega`).
* Analysis (Analyst): the bound is sharp for arithmetic progressions
  (`A = {0,1,…,m−1}` gives `kA = {0,…,k(m−1)}` of size exactly `k(m−1)+1` while
  that stays `< p`).  Saturation happens at `k = ⌈(p−1)/(|A|−1)⌉`.
* Critique (Critic): the corollary `sumset_generates` is non-vacuous — it needs
  `|A| ≥ 2`; for `|A| = 1` (singleton) `kA` is a singleton forever, which the
  bound `min(p, k·0+1) = 1` correctly predicts.  No hidden triviality: the proof
  uses genuine induction and Cauchy–Davenport, not `decide`.
* Synthesis (PI): `card_sumIter_ge` is the headline growth law;
  `sumset_generates` is the saturation corollary tying it to "filling space".
-/

open Finset Pointwise

namespace KakeyaKatzTao

/-- Iterated sumset: `sumIter A k = A + A + ⋯ + A` (`k+1` copies, so
`sumIter A 0 = A`). -/
def sumIter {p : ℕ} (A : Finset (ZMod p)) : ℕ → Finset (ZMod p)
  | 0 => A
  | (k + 1) => A + sumIter A k

@[simp] theorem sumIter_zero {p : ℕ} (A : Finset (ZMod p)) : sumIter A 0 = A := rfl

theorem sumIter_succ {p : ℕ} (A : Finset (ZMod p)) (k : ℕ) :
    sumIter A (k + 1) = A + sumIter A k := rfl

/-
The iterated sumset of a nonempty set is nonempty.
-/
theorem sumIter_nonempty {p : ℕ} {A : Finset (ZMod p)} (hA : A.Nonempty) (k : ℕ) :
    (sumIter A k).Nonempty := by
  induction' k with k ih <;> simp_all +decide [ sumIter_succ ]

/-
Any subset of `ZMod p` has at most `p` elements.
-/
theorem card_le_p {p : ℕ} [NeZero p] (A : Finset (ZMod p)) : A.card ≤ p := by
  simpa using Finset.card_le_univ A

/-
**Iterated Cauchy–Davenport growth.** For a prime `p` and nonempty
`A ⊆ ZMod p`, the `k`-fold sumset satisfies `|kA| ≥ min(p, k(|A|−1)+1)`.
-/
theorem card_sumIter_ge {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) {A : Finset (ZMod p)}
    (hA : A.Nonempty) (k : ℕ) :
    min p (k * (A.card - 1) + 1) ≤ (sumIter A k).card := by
  induction' k with k ih;
  · grind +suggestions;
  · have := @ZMod.cauchy_davenport;
    convert this hp hA ( sumIter_nonempty hA k ) |> le_trans _ using 1;
    grind

/-
**Saturation / generation.** If `A ⊆ ZMod p` has at least two elements, then
once `k ≥ p − 1` the iterated sumset is all of `ZMod p` (it has `p` elements).
-/
theorem sumset_generates {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) {A : Finset (ZMod p)}
    (hA : 2 ≤ A.card) {k : ℕ} (hk : p - 1 ≤ k) :
    (sumIter A k).card = p := by
  refine' le_antisymm _ _;
  · haveI := Fact.mk hp; exact le_trans ( Finset.card_le_univ _ ) ( by simp +decide ) ;
  · refine' le_trans _ ( card_sumIter_ge hp ( Finset.card_pos.mp ( by linarith ) ) k );
    exact le_min le_rfl ( by nlinarith [ Nat.sub_add_cancel hp.pos, Nat.sub_pos_of_lt hA ] )

end KakeyaKatzTao
